summaries.summary: Security pass over the new frontends (web, the /agent broker console, admin), the seams between them and the API, the stage-2 endpoints and the nginx/PM2 deploy kit. I found four issues: two medium, two low. No XSS sinks: the only dangerouslySetInnerHTML is the JSON-LD helper, which escapes '<'. Rich text in notices, terms and policies is parsed into React elements and only http(s) links are allowed. Map markers are DOM portals. Banner, popup, app-store and Kakao-channel URLs and notification links all go through isSafeLinkUrl or a relative-path check. No open redirects: returnTo is checked by safeReturnTo and safeNext (which normalizes dot segments) and by the shared returnToSchema on the API, and OAuth intent=link is tied to the logged-in user and a binding cookie. There are no server actions and no non-mock route handlers apart from /healthz. All 194 mock-api handlers sit behind mockGuard, either directly or through a helper (meGuard, agencyContext, listingsContext, agencyGuard, ownerGuard, modGate, mockAdmin). The /dev pages call notFound() in production, and the e2e-auth module only loads with NODE_ENV=test and E2E_FAKE_OAUTH=1. A grep of the built .next/static bundles found no secrets, and deploy.sh passes only NEXT_PUBLIC_* variables to the build. The stage-2 endpoints I checked are scoped to the caller's user or agency: /me favorites and interest-regions, me/deal-requests, my-agency, proposals, and admin permissions. Deal-request contact details are shown only to agencies holding an active grant, and the public listing selects leave out the 호 (unit) number. The problems are in the seams: (1) server-side rendering never passes the visitor's IP to the API, so anonymous SSR shares one 127.0.0.1 rate-limit bucket that anyone can use up; (2) the API's CORS and CSRF origin allowlist trusts the public site's origin for the admin API; (3) both Next apps let the image optimizer fetch anything on the API's loopback port in production; (4) the only script CSP is Report-Only, and it is already missing the new Kakao postcode host. Scratch dir /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-house/c2396f93-7331-5f3f-8b66-a9630e5b89f0/scratchpad/audit/ was not used; no repo files were changed.

Performance audit of the frontends, the integration seams and the deploy kit. I edited nothing in the repo. I worked from the existing apps/web/.next and apps/admin/.next build outputs (Next 15.5.29), the source, the house_dev index catalog and the nginx/PM2 templates. I found 6 issues.

1. **High: `next/image` is broken in production for every `/media` image.** The rewrite target for `/media` is fixed when the app is built. `deploy.sh` never passes `MEDIA_ORIGIN` to the build, so the image optimizer fetches from the API, which has no `/media` route.
2. **Medium: about 130 KB gzipped of unneeded JavaScript on every page.** `@house/shared` is published as CommonJS only. Its barrel cannot be tree-shaken, and it pulls in a second, CommonJS copy of zod with every language's error messages. This hits all web pages, the home page included, and every admin page.
3. **Medium: all server-side rendering shares one rate-limit bucket.** Next's server-side calls to the API carry no visitor IP, so they all count as 127.0.0.1 for each route. nginx puts no rate limit on page requests. One scraper can use up that bucket and make first-time page renders fail for everyone.
4. **Medium: the `/search` page cache grows without limit.** Every distinct `q` is written to the Next fetch cache on disk. `deploy.sh` copies that cache into each new release.
5. **Low: view counts are distorted by server-side rendering.** The `/complex/[id]` page never records a view, while the server-side read of `/listings/:id` adds a fake view to every listing.
6. **Low: `/_next/static` is served by Node.** Files are compressed on every request in the Next process instead of by nginx.

These checked out with nothing to report:
- The stage-2 API endpoints (home summary, popular regions, search suggest, similar listings, complex nearby/agencies, admin stats/search/dashboard, agency inbox) use batched queries, not one query per row. Their results are cached in Redis and invalidated by version bump where needed.
- The indexes these queries need exist (GiST on location, trigram on names, the composite status indexes).
- The map SDK is loaded lazily, fonts come through `next/font`, and the home page fetches its 9 data blocks in parallel with 5 s timeouts.
- nginx has keepalive upstreams, HTTP/2 and gzip, and `/media` is served immutable.

The dev DB holds only about 200 listings, so EXPLAIN plans would not reflect production. I checked the index catalog instead.

Read-only compliance audit (Korean legal lens) of apps/web (user site and /agent console), apps/admin and packages/ui, plus the stage-2 API modules they call (listings, agencies, deal-requests, auth/terms, admin) and the deploy kit. No repo files were edited.

What already holds up (checked, no findings):
- 표시·광고: the listing detail shows the full 명시사항 per office (BrokersCard, ContactDialog, buildDisclosure). The public payload never carries 호.
- 중개보조원 on listings: listing contacts and the agency page are limited to licensed members (resolveContact, memberDeparted, isAdvertisableMember).
- Admin PII: lists are masked, and unmasked detail and document views write pii-view audit rows.
- Signup consents: 만 14세 is gated before submit, 필수/선택 are labelled, MARKETING and LOCATION can only be optional.
- Banners: every slot carries an AD badge and rel=sponsored. Popups have no advertiser field.
- No third-party analytics or cookies are loaded.
- Basic accessibility: lang="ko", the carousel can be paused, image alt text is handled.

Findings that remain, all with code evidence:
- **High:**
  - Deal-request retention does not match the consent text. Users are told data is kept until 30 days after the request ends; the code keeps contacts for 90 days, and partly forever.
  - Every agency in the region gets the exact road address, coordinates, floor, photos and description of a 내놓기 request before any contact grant. The consent notice promises only an approximate location at that stage.
- **Medium:**
  - The consent version recorded is the one current at submit time, not the text the user saw. The notice text shown is hardcoded in the frontend.
  - Rejected agency applications and their documents are never purged, although the notice promises deletion 1 year after rejection.
  - A 중개보조원 can write a proposal. The requester sees the assistant's name, and the API returns the assistant's phone, with nothing saying the person is a 중개보조원.
  - The "내 위치" buttons use device location without checking the LOCATION (위치기반서비스) consent. The position then goes into the URL and into API request logs.
- **Low:**
  - The 개인정보처리방침 is bundled into a required consent, so any policy update blocks every member until they re-consent.
  - The footer has no 호스팅서비스 제공자 (전자상거래법 시행령 제7조).
  - The listing JSON-LD gives a monthly-rent-only price, marks reserved listings InStock, and names 전라남도, which conflicts with D1.
  - Cards, markers and meta descriptions use 평 as the only unit.
  - The report dialog takes an optional phone number without saying it is kept for 180 days.

confirmed.title: SSR never forwards the visitor's IP to the API, so all anonymous server-rendered page loads share one per-route 127.0.0.1 rate-limit bucket that one attacker can exhaust
confirmed.evidence: apps/web/src/lib/api/server.ts:20-26 (serverGet) and :51-66 (serverGetAuthed) call apiFetch with no x-forwarded-for header; grep finds no 'x-forwarded-for' anywhere in apps/web/src or apps/admin/src. ecosystem.config.cjs sets INTERNAL_API_URL=http://127.0.0.1:<API_PORT>, so SSR calls skip nginx. apps/api/src/common/throttle/house-throttler.guard.ts:26-29 says 'the SSR server must forward the visitor's X-Forwarded-For ... so loopback-trusted calls are keyed by the real client', and getTracker (:45-49) falls back to `ip:${req.ip}`. With TRUST_PROXY=loopback (deploy/install.sh:706) and no header, req.ip is 127.0.0.1. The default throttler is 1200 req / 60 s per route per tracker (apps/api/src/config/env.schema.ts:108-111). nginx puts no limit_req on page routes: deploy/nginx/snippets/house-web-locations.conf:31 `location / { proxy_pass http://house_web; }`. apps/web/src/app/(listing)/listing/[id]/page.tsx:41-61 rethrows every ApiError except 404/400, so a 429 renders the error page. apps/web/src/app/(agencies)/agencies/page.tsx:39 builds the API query from searchParams, so each new query string misses the cache.
confirmed.scenario: From one IP, the attacker requests https://<domain>/listing/<random-uuid> (or /agencies?region=<varied>) about 25 times a second. Each unique path misses the ISR and fetch caches, so Next calls GET /api/v1/listings/:id from 127.0.0.1. The throttler checks before validation, so even 400/404 calls count. After 1200 calls in a minute, the 'ip:127.0.0.1' bucket for that route is full. For the rest of the window, every uncached or revalidating listing page for every anonymous visitor (and every search engine crawler) gets 429 from the API and renders the error page. serverGetOr pages (home, agencies) quietly render empty. Signed-in SSR via serverGetAuthed is keyed per user and is not affected.
confirmed.fix: Pass the visitor's IP through on every SSR API call. In serverGet, serverGetAuthed and getServerSession, read `headers()` and send x-forwarded-for set to nginx's value (nginx already sets X-Forwarded-For to $remote_addr; Next listens on 127.0.0.1 only, so the header can be trusted). Also pass user-agent, which the visitor counter and ad bot filter use. Note that reading headers() makes the route dynamic. For ISR/static pages that must stay cacheable, either key SSR calls on a shared internal secret header that HouseThrottlerGuard exempts or gives a much higher bucket, or add a per-IP `limit_req zone=house_pages` on nginx `location /` so a single client cannot cause unbounded uncached SSR fetches.

verdict.reason:
I confirmed this in the code. apps/web/src/lib/api/server.ts: serverGet (lines 20-26) and serverGetAuthed (lines 50-65) send no x-forwarded-for. apiFetch in client.ts (lines 68-86) adds only accept, content-type and CSRF headers. Searching apps/web/src and apps/admin/src finds no code that forwards the client IP; the only forwarded-header read is x-forwarded-host in a mock route. ecosystem.config.cjs:119 sets INTERNAL_API_URL=http://127.0.0.1:${API_PORT}, so SSR calls go straight to the API and skip nginx. The API uses trust proxy = TRUST_PROXY=loopback (configure-app.ts:54, install.sh:706), so with no XFF header req.ip is 127.0.0.1.

HouseThrottlerGuard is the first global APP_GUARD (core.module.ts:42), which means it runs before the ZodValidationPipe, so 400 and 404 calls also count. With no session it keys on `ip:127.0.0.1` (guard :45-49). Its own doc comment (:26-30) says SSR must forward XFF, and the frontend does not. The default limit is 1200 per 60 s per route (env.schema.ts:108-111).

nginx `location /` (house-web-locations.conf:31-34) has no limit_req; only /api/ and the auth routes do. The listing detail page uses generateStaticParams [] and blocking on-demand render, and calls getListing for every new id from generateMetadata (page.tsx:41-61). getListing rethrows every ApiError except 404/400, so a 429 renders the error page. An attacker requesting /listing/<random-uuid> at about 20+ req/s from one IP therefore fills the shared bucket for GET /listings/:id. For the rest of the window, every anonymous visitor and crawler hitting an uncached listing page gets an error. Without this bug, that attacker would only use up their own per-IP bucket.

Two caveats lower the impact. First, the /agencies example is mostly mitigated: page.tsx skips SSR fetches for free-text q, map-area searches and unknown regions. Second, already-cached ISR listing pages most likely keep serving the stale copy when a background revalidation fails. So the realistic damage is to new or uncached listing pages and their SEO crawl, not the whole site. Signed-in SSR is keyed per user and is not affected. Client-side fetches go through nginx with the real IP. That is still a cheap denial-of-service of a core public page from a single IP, so medium stands.

Fix: forward the visitor's IP (and user-agent) from headers() on SSR calls. If the pages must stay cacheable, instead give SSR a secret-header exemption or a higher limit, and add a per-IP limit_req on nginx `location /`.

confirmed.title: The admin API trusts the public site's origin in both CORS (credentialed) and the CSRF Origin check, so any script running on the user site can read the admin CSRF token and act as a logged-in admin
confirmed.evidence: apps/api/src/config/app-config.service.ts:27-32 allowedOrigins = CORS_ORIGINS + PUBLIC_BASE_URL origin + ADMIN_BASE_URL origin (install.sh:709 sets CORS_ORIGINS="${BASE},${ADMIN_BASE}"). apps/api/src/bootstrap/configure-app.ts:77-81 `enableCors({ origin: (o,cb)=>cb(null, o===undefined||origins.has(o)), credentials: true })`. The CSRF guard uses the same set for every path, admin included (apps/api/src/common/auth/csrf.guard.ts:27,41). apps/api/src/modules/auth/admin/admin-auth.controller.ts:53-61 GET /admin/auth/csrf returns `{ csrfToken: session.csrfToken }` in the body. Auth cookies are SameSite=Lax, host-only (session.service.ts:209-216; install.sh:712 COOKIE_DOMAIN=""). admin.<domain> and <domain> are same-site, so the house_admin_sid cookie goes with credentialed fetches from the public site. The public site loads third-party scripts into its origin: apps/web/src/components/map/naver.ts:76 (oapi.map.naver.com) and apps/web/src/features/w-deal/lib/daum-postcode.ts:10-12 (t1.kakaocdn.net, overridable by env). The only script CSP is Report-Only (deploy/nginx/snippets/house-csp.conf:5).
confirmed.scenario: An admin is logged into https://admin.<domain> and also browses https://<domain>. Any script running on the public origin can do the following: an XSS bug in the large user-generated surface, a compromised Naver Maps or Kakao postcode CDN script, or a malicious NEXT_PUBLIC_POSTCODE_SCRIPT_URL. It calls fetch('https://admin.<domain>/api/v1/admin/auth/csrf',{credentials:'include'}). The browser sends house_admin_sid (same-site, Lax), and the API answers with Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://<domain> plus credentials, so the script reads csrfToken. It then sends PATCH/POST/DELETE to /api/v1/admin/* (users suspend, site-settings, banners, admins with ADMINS_MANAGE) with x-csrf-token. That passes the Origin allowlist and the token check. A compromise of the public site becomes a back-office takeover, defeating the separate admin subdomain, the nginx admin IP allow-list (the admin's own browser is on it) and TOTP (the session is already verified).
confirmed.fix: Split the origin policy by path. For /api/v1/admin/* (use isAdminPath), CORS and the CSRF guard should accept only new URL(ADMIN_BASE_URL).origin. For user endpoints, accept only PUBLIC_BASE_URL. Simplest: in enableCors use the `origin` callback with the request (cors' `(req, cb)` delegate form) to choose the allowed set by path, and in CsrfGuard check `isAdminPath(req) ? adminOrigin : webOrigin`. Both frontends are same-origin with the API through nginx, so neither needs cross-origin access at all; consider dropping credentialed CORS altogether. Optionally make the admin cookies SameSite=Strict.

verdict.reason:
I confirmed this in the code. AppConfig.allowedOrigins (apps/api/src/config/app-config.service.ts:27-32) joins CORS_ORIGINS, the PUBLIC_BASE_URL origin and the ADMIN_BASE_URL origin into one set. install.sh:709 writes both origins into CORS_ORIGINS. configure-app.ts:77-85 turns on credentialed CORS for that set on every path; it never looks at the path. CsrfGuard (csrf.guard.ts:21-28, 40-41) checks Origin against the same set for every route, admin routes included. Its only other check is the session token.

GET /admin/auth/csrf (admin-auth.controller.ts:53-61) is @Public, uses the admin session that comes from house_admin_sid, and puts csrfToken in the response body. SessionKind is chosen by isAdminPath (session.service.ts:101). Cookies are SameSite=Lax, path=/, and host-only (COOKIE_DOMAIN="" per install.sh:712, baseCookie at session.service.ts:209-216). <domain> and admin.<domain> are same-site, so a credentialed fetch from the public origin to admin.<domain> carries the admin cookie. The API then answers with ACAO=https://<domain> and credentials allowed, so the script can read the token.

Nothing else blocks this. nginx admin-locations (house-admin-locations.conf) passes /api/ straight through, with no Origin or Sec-Fetch filtering and no CORS override. AdminIpGuard (admin-ip.guard.ts) only checks req.ip, and that is the admin's own browser IP, which is on the allow-list. No admin path is limited to the admin origin.

Why CORS is the key enabler: house_admin_sid and house_csrf are host-only to admin.<domain>. So a same-origin call from <domain> would send no admin cookie, and the public site cannot read the CSRF cookie. Without the public origin in the credentialed CORS allowlist, the chain fails. Neither frontend needs cross-origin access, because both reach the API same-origin through nginx.

Severity stays medium. The attack needs script execution on the public origin first: an XSS bug, a compromised Naver or Kakao script, or a bad env URL. Given that, it removes the isolation between the public site and the back office, so a public-site compromise becomes full admin actions with an already TOTP-verified session. The fix is to pick allowed origins by path: admin paths accept only the ADMIN_BASE_URL origin, other paths accept PUBLIC_BASE_URL. This applies to both the CORS delegate and CsrfGuard. Alternatively, drop credentialed CORS altogether.

confirmed.title: next/image optimizer cannot load any /media image in production (rewrite points at the API, which does not serve /media)
confirmed.evidence: apps/web/next.config.mjs:31-33: `API_ORIGIN = INTERNAL_API_URL || 'http://127.0.0.1:4000'`, `MEDIA_ORIGIN = process.env.MEDIA_ORIGIN || API_ORIGIN`. Line 89 has the rewrite `/media/:path*` -> `${MEDIA_ORIGIN}/media/:path*`. Next writes rewrites into routes-manifest.json at build time; the current build has destination `http://127.0.0.1:4000/media/:path*`. deploy/deploy.sh:233-238 passes only `NODE_ENV` and `NEXT_PUBLIC_*` to the build. MEDIA_ORIGIN is not set anywhere in deploy/ or ecosystem.config.cjs. The API serves nothing under /media: configure-app.ts:87 sets the global prefix api/v1, media.controller.ts is under /api/v1/media, and there is no static serving. Public files are served only by nginx from disk (deploy/nginx/snippets/house-media.conf.template). apps/web/src/lib/media.ts:17 marks every `/media/` src as optimizable (`unoptimized: false`), so <Image> requests `/_next/image?url=/media/...`. docs/frontend-integration/foundation.md:66-68 says MEDIA_ORIGIN must point at nginx in production, but the deploy kit never sets it. The e2e stack starts a separate media server (scripts/e2e-stack.sh:43, 115), so the e2e tests cannot catch this. apps/admin/next.config.mjs:32-91 has the same rewrite.
confirmed.scenario: After a normal deploy, the browser requests /_next/image?url=%2Fmedia%2Flistings%2Fabc.webp&w=640. The optimizer follows the rewrite to 127.0.0.1:4000/media/... and the API answers 404, so the optimizer returns an error. Every optimized image fails: listing photos and cards, agency logos and covers, complex photos and banners. The OG and JSON-LD URLs still work, so the damage only shows in the browser.
confirmed.fix: Point the optimizer at nginx. One way: add a loopback-only nginx server (`listen 127.0.0.1:8088; location ~ ^/media/... { alias {{UPLOAD_PUBLIC}}/$1; }`) and add MEDIA_ORIGIN=http://127.0.0.1:8088 to BUILD_ENV in deploy/deploy.sh for both web and admin. The API already generates webp thumb and large variants, so the other way is to render /media images with `unoptimized` (change isOptimizableImage) and pick the right variant URL. That skips the optimizer's sharp CPU work and its disk cache. Add a deploy smoke test that GETs one /_next/image?url=/media/... and expects 200 image/*.

verdict.reason:
I tried to refute this finding and could not. Each link in the chain checks out in the code:

1. **The rewrite falls back to the API.** apps/web/next.config.mjs:31-33 sets `MEDIA_ORIGIN = process.env.MEDIA_ORIGIN || API_ORIGIN`, and API_ORIGIN defaults to http://127.0.0.1:4000. Line 89 rewrites `/media/:path*` to `${MEDIA_ORIGIN}/media/:path*`. apps/admin/next.config.mjs:33 and :91 do the same.

2. **The deploy kit never sets MEDIA_ORIGIN.** Searching the whole repo, MEDIA_ORIGIN appears only in scripts/e2e-stack.sh, a commented line in apps/web/.env.example and the docs. deploy.sh:233-237 passes only `NODE_ENV` and the `NEXT_PUBLIC_*` keys from .env to the build. turbo.json's globalPassThroughEnv does not list it either.

3. **The optimizer does follow the rewrite.** In Next 15.5.29, next-server.js:822-841 fetches a relative image URL with `fetchInternalImage(..., handleInternalReq)`, which calls `this.routerServerHandler`. That handler applies rewrites, including ones that proxy to an external host. So `/_next/image?url=/media/...` fetches http://127.0.0.1:4000/media/....

4. **The API serves nothing under /media.** configure-app.ts:87 calls `setGlobalPrefix(API_PREFIX)` (api/v1). There is no useStaticAssets, ServeStatic or express.static anywhere in apps/api/src. scripts/e2e/media-server.mjs:3 says it outright: "the API itself never serves files". Production API_PORT defaults to 4000 (ecosystem.config.cjs), so the fallback really does hit the API, which answers 404.

5. **Media URLs are relative `/media/...` paths.** install.sh:718 sets `MEDIA_BASE_URL=/media`.

6. **Nothing in nginx catches /_next/image first.** It has no location for that path, so it reaches Next through `location /` in house-web-locations.conf. Only nginx serves /media, from disk (house-media.conf.template).

7. **Real image components take the optimized path.** apps/web/src/lib/media.ts:17-22 returns `unoptimized: false` for `/media/` URLs. ListingMiniCard, NewListingsSection, AgenciesSection, NoticePopup and BannerPicture all use `imageProps`. a-agency MediaImage and admin m-moderation MediaImage also leave real `/media/**` images optimized.

Result: after a normal deploy, every optimized `/media` image fails with an upstream 404 error. That covers listing cards, agency logos and covers, and banners on the web site and in the admin app. The e2e tests cannot catch it because they set MEDIA_ORIGIN to a separate media server.

Severity stays high because user-visible images break across the production site. This is really a correctness bug, not a performance issue.

The proposed fix is sound. One option is to build with MEDIA_ORIGIN pointing at an nginx listener bound to loopback only. MEDIA_ORIGIN would need adding to BUILD_ENV, because rewrites are written into routes-manifest at build time. The other option is to stop optimizing `/media` images and use the webp variants the API already generates. A deploy smoke test on `/_next/image?url=/media/...` should be added either way.

confirmed.title: @house/shared is CommonJS-only: every web and admin page ships a second, untree-shaken zod with all locales plus the whole shared barrel (about 130 KB gzipped)
confirmed.evidence: packages/shared/package.json has main/exports `./dist/index.js`, built by `tsc` to CommonJS. dist/index.js is `__exportStar(require("./enums")) ... require("./schemas")`, which webpack cannot tree-shake. apps/web/src/lib/api/client.ts:1 imports only `{ ErrorCode }`, but the root layout manifest (apps/web/.next/app-build-manifest.json '/layout') still contains: static/chunks/6642-d83a4521fc1825db.js, 478 KB raw / 97 KB gz, CommonJS zod (`__createBinding`) with 63 `localeError` tables (Lithuanian and other locales); static/chunks/8435-4d3e747feee1a03c.js, 134 KB raw / 36 KB gz, all of @house/shared; and static/chunks/3135-d59e10cdf4f27e99.js, 96 KB raw / 27 KB gz, the ESM zod the web app imports itself. The root layout's first-load JS is 288 KB gz (1.13 MB raw), and '/' is 339 KB gz. Every admin page also carries 66 locale tables (apps/admin/.next, e.g. /(console)/banners/page at 360 KB gz).
confirmed.scenario: A mobile visitor on 3G/LTE opening any page, including the home page and SEO landing pages, downloads and parses roughly 600 KB of extra raw JS (zod error messages in about 45 languages, plus every shared schema). That adds main-thread parse and compile time before hydration, which raises TBT/INP, delays hydration, and costs Core Web Vitals and Naver/Google ranking on the pages built for SEO.
confirmed.fix: Publish shared as ESM as well. Emit an ESM build (tsc with module ESNext to dist/esm, or tsup) and use exports `{ ".": { "types": ..., "import": "./dist/esm/index.js", "require": "./dist/index.js" } }` with `sideEffects: false`. The frontends then resolve zod's ESM entry once, the locales drop out, and unused schemas are tree-shaken. The API keeps the CommonJS build. Another option is to point the frontends at the sources (`"import": "./src/index.ts"` plus `transpilePackages: ['@house/shared']`). Afterwards, check that no chunk contains `localeError` more than once.

verdict.reason:
I could not refute this finding. The source and the build output both confirm it.

**Source**
- `packages/shared/package.json` exports only `./dist/index.js` (no `import` condition). It is built by `tsc` to CommonJS: `dist/index.js` is `__exportStar(require('./enums'))` and so on for 12 modules.
- Shared's `require('zod')` resolves through zod 4.6.7's `"require": "./index.cjs"` condition. The apps' own `import 'zod'` resolves `"import": "./index.js"`. Webpack therefore bundles two separate zod copies.
- `apps/web/next.config` lists only `@house/ui` in `transpilePackages`, not `@house/shared`.

**Web build** (`apps/web/.next`, production build with hashed chunks)
The `/layout` manifest entry includes three relevant chunks:

| Chunk | Raw | Gzipped | Contents |
|---|---|---|---|
| `6642-d83a4521fc1825db.js` | 490 KB | 100 KB | CommonJS zod: `__createBinding`/`__importStar` wrappers, 63 `localeError` tables, Lithuanian `Neteisingas` and Chinese `无效输入` strings present |
| `8435-4d3e747feee1a03c.js` | 137 KB | 37 KB | The whole shared barrel: `ERROR_MESSAGES` (x30), `ACTION_CONSENT_TERMS`, `agencyRegisterSchema`, `COOKIE_NAMES` |
| `3135-d59e10cdf4f27e99.js` | 98 KB | 28 KB | The ESM zod, with no locale strings |

This chunk is pulled in because `apps/web/src/lib/api/client.ts:1` imports `{ ErrorCode }` from `@house/shared`, along with many other `src/lib` modules.

**Admin build** (`apps/admin/.next`)
- `/(console)/layout` and `/(console)/banners/page` both include `static/chunks/7434-b7a214f1c715b8ff.js`: 558 KB raw, with 66 `localeError` tables.
- First-load JS: banners page 360 KB gzipped, console layout 306 KB gzipped.

**Severity**
About 100-130 KB gzipped (roughly 600 KB raw) of duplicate, untree-shaken JS ships on every page, including the public SEO pages. That is a real Core Web Vitals and parse-time cost, but it does not break any function, so medium is right. The `.next` output may be slightly stale while other agents edit, but the package config alone guarantees the double bundling.

**Fix**

confirmed.title: All Next server-side API reads share one per-route `ip:127.0.0.1` throttle bucket, and nginx does not rate-limit page requests
confirmed.evidence: apps/web/src/lib/api/server.ts:21-26 (serverGet) and apps/web/src/lib/api/client.ts:68-87 send only `accept` (plus a cookie for authed requests), never X-Forwarded-For. apps/api/src/common/throttle/house-throttler.guard.ts:24-31 acknowledges that "the SSR server must forward the visitor's X-Forwarded-For", and line 48 falls back to `ip:${req.ip}`, which is 127.0.0.1 for Next's calls (TRUST_PROXY=loopback, configure-app.ts:54). The global limit is THROTTLE_LIMIT=1200 per THROTTLE_TTL_MS=60000 per handler (env.schema.ts:108-111; @nestjs/throttler keys by class, handler and tracker). deploy/nginx/snippets/house-web-locations.conf:31-34 (`location /`) has no limit_req, unlike /api/ at line 24. The pages render on demand: /listing/[id] and /complex/[id] use generateStaticParams() => [] with ISR, and /agency/[id], /agencies and /search are dynamic, each with 2 to 8 server-side fetches per render (e.g. app/(site)/complex/[id]/page.tsx:100-136).
confirmed.scenario: A scraper requests /listing/<distinct uuid> or /complex/<id> about 25 times a second, unthrottled at nginx. Each cache miss calls GET /api/v1/listings/:id from 127.0.0.1, and after 1200 calls in a minute the API answers 429 to the shared bucket. For the rest of that window, every real visitor's first render of a listing that is not cached fails. getListing rethrows non-404 ApiErrors, so the page returns a 500. Crawlers indexing new listings get errors too. This is a cheap way to deny service, and it also wastes CPU, because nginx caps only /api/.
confirmed.fix: Choose one of these. (a) Give the Next servers their own path: have the API skip the throttler or use a much higher bucket for loopback requests that carry a shared secret header such as X-Internal-SSR set from the PM2 env, and forward the visitor IP only on uncached dynamic renders. (b) Forward `x-forwarded-for` from headers() on dynamic routes. Option (b) cannot work for ISR or background revalidation, so (a) is still needed. Also add a generous per-IP `limit_req` zone to nginx `location /` on the web and admin servers, for example 10r/s with burst 50 to suit carrier CGNAT.

verdict.reason:
I confirmed the finding against the code; nothing elsewhere handles it.

How the SSR calls reach the API:
- Server-side fetches go straight to INTERNAL_API_URL=http://127.0.0.1:4000 (apps/web/src/lib/api/config.ts:21). They skip nginx, so no X-Forwarded-For is added.
- serverGet (apps/web/src/lib/api/server.ts:20-26) and apiFetch (client.ts:68) send only `accept` and any caller headers. Nothing under apps/web/src mentions x-forwarded-for.
- With TRUST_PROXY=loopback (env.schema.ts:27, configure-app.ts:54), req.ip is therefore 127.0.0.1.
- HouseThrottlerGuard.getTracker returns `ip:${req.ip}` for anonymous requests (house-throttler.guard.ts:48). Its own comment (lines 26-30) says SSR must forward XFF, but the web app never does.

How the bucket works:
- In @nestjs/throttler 6.8.0, generateKey is sha256 of `${class}-${handler}-${name}-${tracker}` (throttler.guard.js:169-171). So one bucket is shared per handler by every SSR call.
- That bucket allows 1200 per 60s (core.module.ts:27-36, env.schema.ts:108-111). There is no skipIf and no loopback exemption.

Why the bucket can be drained from outside:
- The nginx `location /` block (house-web-locations.conf:31-34) has no limit_req. Only /api/ and auth do (house-upstreams.conf.template:30-31).
- /listing/[id] uses generateStaticParams => [] with revalidate=60, and serverGet is called on each uncached id (listing/[id]/page.tsx:35-62). Random UUIDs are always cache misses.
- The throttler counts a request before the handler runs, so 404 lookups also drain the GET /listings/:id bucket.
- Once the bucket is drained, getListing rethrows any ApiError other than 404 or 400 (line 60-61). A 429 therefore becomes an error page for real visitors and crawlers on any listing that is not cached, for the rest of the window.

Severity stays medium. The DoS takes about 20 requests a second from one IP and hits SEO-critical pages. It does not expose data, and it only affects ISR cache misses.

The fix is correct. Exempt or separately bucket the trusted SSR caller, for example with a shared-secret header from the PM2 env. Forwarding the visitor IP alone cannot cover ISR or background revalidation. Also add a generous per-IP limit_req zone to the nginx `location /` blocks.

confirmed.title: /search caches every distinct q in Next's on-disk fetch cache, with no eviction, and deploy copies that cache into every new release
confirmed.evidence: apps/web/src/features/w-content/api/server.ts:124-147: getSearchResults(q) calls serverGet('/complexes', {query:{q,...}, revalidate: 60}) and serverGet('/agencies', {query:{q,...}, revalidate: 60}). With next.revalidate set, self-hosted `next start` writes each distinct URL to .next/cache/fetch-cache, and nothing deletes those files from disk. The `type` tab changes pageSize, so one q can create up to 8 entries. The agencies page deliberately avoids this (app/(agencies)/agencies/page.tsx: "caching every distinct value would grow the fetch cache without bound"), but /search does not. deploy/deploy.sh:224-231 runs `cp -a "$PREV_RELEASE/apps/$app/.next/cache" ...` on every deploy, so the cache is carried forward forever and each copy takes longer.

Each deploy's `cp -a` slows down along with it.

verdict.reason: Confirmed. apps/web/src/features/w-content/api/server.ts:124-147 sends user-supplied `q` to serverGet('/complexes') and serverGet('/agencies') with `revalidate: 60`. serverGet (apps/web/src/lib/api/server.ts:20-26) turns that into `next: { revalidate, tags }`, and apiFetch passes it through (client.ts:84). On self-hosted Next 15.5.29, any fetch with an explicit revalidate is stored in the incremental cache, even on a dynamic route, and written to .next/cache/fetch-cache. next.config sets no cacheHandler, and nothing on disk is ever evicted. The only bounds on q are normalizeSearchQuery (whitespace cleanup and a length cap) and the API's validation, so random q values produce unlimited distinct cache keys. Empty results come back as 200 and get cached too. One correction: the type tab yields 3 pageSize variants per endpoint, so a single q produces up to 6 entries, not 8. The repo already names this exact risk and avoids it on /agencies (app/(agencies)/agencies/page.tsx:32-35, "caching every distinct value would grow the fetch cache without bound") and on agency/[id] ("bounded fetch-cache cardinality"). /search does not avoid it. Nginx only rate-limits /api and auth locations (house-web-locations.conf:18,24), so the /search page itself is unthrottled. deploy/deploy.sh:224-231 does `cp -a` of the whole previous .next/cache into each new release unless --force is used. Pruning old releases (KEEP_RELEASES=5) deletes old directories, but the newest release always carries the full cache forward, so it never resets. With sustained bot traffic this grows inode and disk use on the shared VPS without limit, and each deploy's copy gets slower. Normal user traffic alone would grow it slowly, so the impact depends on abusive or crawler load. That keeps severity at medium rather than high. I could not refute this finding. Every part of the evidence checks out in the code.

1. **The constant says 90 days.** packages/shared/src/deal-requests/constants.ts:16 sets `CONTACT_RETENTION_DAYS: 90`. Its only consumer is scrubDue in apps/api/src/modules/deal-requests/services/deal-request-maintenance.service.ts:188-189.
2. **The user-facing notices say 30 days.** The web consent text says '요청 종료 후 30일까지' at apps/web/src/features/w-deal/components/form/ContactScopeFields.tsx:307 and :322. The required consent label at :431 says '30일 보관'. The seeded TermsDocument bodies in apps/api/prisma/seed/base.ts:198 and :210 say the same.
3. **No owner decision explains the gap.** I grepped docs/frontend-integration/DECISIONS.md for retention, 보유 and 90 and found nothing.
4. **No other job deletes this data at 30 days.** I found no deleteMany, purge or discardPhotos call for deal requests other than eraseWithdrawn.
5. **The scheduled scrub only clears contact fields.** scrubDue (:208-210) clears contactName, contactPhone and addressDetail, and only for requests that ended at least 90 days ago and whose owner has not withdrawn. verdict.reason:
I could not refute this; the code confirms it.

1. **The version is fetched at submit time, not when the form loads.** apps/web/src/lib/api/consents.ts:15-42 calls GET /terms/:type and sends whatever `version` comes back. The comment says this happens "right before the submission so the server never refuses a stale version". Three callers use it this way: features/w-deal/api/client.ts:67 and features/a-agency/api/queries.ts:141 and :222.

2. **The notices users read are hardcoded and never loaded from the TermsDocument.**
   - ContactScopeFields.tsx:298-325 holds `privacyRows` and `provideRows`, rendered by `ConsentItem`.
   - features/a-agency/lib/application.ts:245-256 holds `APPLICATION_PRIVACY_NOTICE` and `JOIN_PRIVACY_NOTICE`, rendered by PrivacySummary.tsx.
   - The only links in these notices go to ROUTES.terms('privacy'), the general privacy policy, not the purpose document.

3. **The hardcoded text already differs from the seeded v1.0 documents** (apps/api/prisma/seed/base.ts:169-213).
   - The PRIVACY_AGENCY_APPLICATION seed lists 이메일, 중개사무소 등록번호 and 제출 서류(등록증 등). application.ts:246 leaves out the first two and says only 제출 서류.
   - The PRIVACY_AGENCY_JOIN seed includes 직함. JOIN_PRIVACY_NOTICE leaves it out, and its purpose text is shorter.

4. **This divergence is the planned course, not a one-off.** The seed says it is a 견본 (sample) that the operator will replace through the admin with a reviewed version (base.ts:216-217, 231). After that, any admin edit changes the recorded version, while users still see the old hardcoded text.

The server only checks that the submitted version is the current one (DECISIONS.md D8). It cannot know what text the user was shown, so the Consent rows record agreement to a document the user may never have seen. That weakens the operator's ability to prove informed consent under 개인정보 보호법 제15조② and 제17조②.

**Severity: medium.** This is a real compliance gap in proving consent, not a vulnerability that exposes data. The recorded version always exists and is current, and the hardcoded notices do cover the statutory headings.

**Fix:** Load the purpose document when the form mounts and render its content, or generate the notice from it, next to the checkbox. Submit the version that was loaded. If the server rejects that version as stale, show the new text and ask the user to agree again.

ProposalCard.tsx:150-151 renders '담당 {memberName}' with no 중개보조원 label, next to the recommended listings. (5) The rest of the codebase deliberately keeps 중개보조원 out of the user-facing side: agency-listings.service.ts:581-595 picks only an OWNER or licensed contact for ads, mayBeAdvertised is defined in listings/ports/agency-membership.port.ts:28, and agency-public.service.ts:197-205 filters to OWNER or isLicensed. AgencyPageView.tsx:407 labels 중개보조원 explicitly. agency-members.service.ts:252-254 makes every joining member isLicensed=false. So the default path is a 중개보조원 sending a proposal and appearing to the requester as '담당 X' with no disclosure. This is the inconsistency the finding describes, on a seam the listings side already guards. Correction: the phone the UI shows is the agency's (ProposalCard.tsx:233 uses a.phone, and proposalFromWire maps it from agency.phone). The member's own mobile is not rendered. It is only present in the raw API JSON (agent.phone), so the requester could still read it from the response. Severity stays medium. There is a real 고지/표시 gap on the requester-facing surface, which conflicts with the 제18조의4 notice duty and the 18조의2 display rule the code applies elsewhere. It is not high, because the agency name, 대표 and agency phone are still shown correctly and the member's phone is not displayed in the UI. Fix as proposed: in ProposalsService.create, either restrict authorship with mayBeAdvertised or show the OWNER or a licensed member as the agent; otherwise add isLicensed/role to ProposalAgentView and render '중개보조원'. Also drop member.phone from the requester view unless it is needed.

confirmed.title: The '내 위치' feature uses device location without the 위치기반서비스 consent the site collects, and puts the position in the URL and API requests
confirmed.evidence: MapSearchPage.tsx:487-505 locate() calls navigator.geolocation.getCurrentPosition and then setView({ center: centerOn(me, …) }). AgencySearch.tsx:340-353 does the same and writes `view: { center: here }` into the URL state. Neither checks the member's LOCATION consent. TermsType.LOCATION is collected at signup (features/w-auth/lib/consents.ts:8,16) but is never read anywhere in apps/web/src or apps/api/src outside terms bookkeeping. Anonymous visitors can use the button too. The view is serialized as `?c=lat,lng` at 1e-5 precision (lib/map/url-state.ts:148, lib/map/geo.ts:101-102) and sent as a bbox to GET /listings (features/w-map/api/queries.ts:28-33). nginx access logs keep it (deploy/nginx/house.conf.template:47). This contradicts the seeded LOCATION text ('회원이 허용한 경우에만 현재 위치를 사용하며, 위치정보는 저장하지 않습니다', seed base.ts) and shared/admin/rules.ts:114 ('only when the member allows it').
confirmed.scenario: A member who declined the 선택 위치기반서비스 약관 at signup, or a logged-out visitor, taps 내 위치. The browser prompt is the only gate. The site then uses their position, sends it to the server, logs it in nginx for the log-rotation period, and puts it in a shareable URL. Under 위치정보법 제18조/제19조 a 위치기반서비스사업자 must obtain the subject's consent under its 이용약관 before using personal location data, and operating such a service needs a 신고 (제9조).
confirmed.fix: Before calling geolocation, check consent. For members, read the LOCATION consent from /me/consents and offer an inline agree dialog with the LOCATION document. For anonymous users, show a one-time notice with the 약관 link, or hide the button. Do not write the device position into the URL: keep it client-side and round it before it goes into the bbox or URL, or exclude query strings from the nginx access_log for /api/v1/listings. Confirm the operator's 위치기반서비스사업 신고 status, or change the feature so no position leaves the device, and align the LOCATION text with what the code does.

verdict.reason:
I could not refute it. Every factual claim checks out in the code. MapSearchPage.tsx:487-505 locate() calls navigator.geolocation.getCurrentPosition. If the position is inside the service radius, it calls setView({ center: centerOn(me, zoom, openStop), zoom }). setView is the URL-synced map state (line 143). AgencySearch.tsx:340-353 writes view.center = the exact device position into URL state with 'replace'. serializeMapView (lib/map/url-state.ts:148) writes c=lat,lng rounded to 1e-5 by roundCoord (lib/map/geo.ts:101-102), which is about 1 m. The bbox derived from that view goes to /map/search and /listings. In apps/web, LOCATION appears only in the signup consent list, the terms labels and fixtures. No code checks the member's LOCATION consent before geolocation, and logged-out visitors get the same button. The seeded LOCATION body (apps/api/prisma/seed/base.ts:159: '회원이 허용한 경우에만 현재 위치를 사용하며, 위치정보는 저장하지 않습니다') and the comment at packages/shared/src/admin/rules.ts:114 describe consent-gated use. The code does not gate it, so a member who declined the optional 약관 is treated the same as one who agreed. The nginx web server block has an access_log (deploy/nginx/house.conf.template:47), so requests carrying the center or bbox are logged with their query strings.

Mitigating points:
- The browser permission prompt still gates access.
- Positions outside the Suncheon radius are dropped.
- On MapSearchPage the URL center is offset by centerOn, so it is only near the device position, not exactly it.

Because of these, the claim that the position is 'sent to the server' is approximate: it arrives as a viewport around the device position. The legal points about 신고 (위치정보법 제9조) are context, not code evidence. Still, the consent the site collects and the policy text both disagree with what the code does. That makes this a concrete compliance gap, and medium severity fits: no security exploit, but there is regulatory and privacy-policy exposure.

low.title: next/image in production may fetch any path on the API's loopback port (http://127.0.0.1:4000/**), giving anonymous users a server-side request path that bypasses nginx's /api rate limit
low.evidence: apps/web/next.config.mjs:78-81 and apps/admin/next.config.mjs:80-83 always include remotePatterns { protocol:'http', hostname:'localhost'|'127.0.0.1', port:'4000', pathname:'/**' }, with no isProd guard. Media URLs are same-origin /media/* paths, so these entries are dev leftovers. Next 15.5.29's optimizer (node_modules/next/dist/server/image-optimizer.js:638 hasRemoteMatch, :899-922 fetchExternalImage) fetches the URL server-side and returns the upstream status code. /_next/image is served by nginx `location /` (house-web-locations.conf:31), which has no limit_req, unlike `location /api/` (zone house_api).
low.scenario: The attacker requests https://<domain>/_next/image?url=http%3A%2F%2F127.0.0.1%3A4000%2Fapi%2Fv1%2Flistings%2F<x>&w=64&q=75 with varying <x>. Each request makes the web server call the API from 127.0.0.1, with no cookie and no X-Forwarded-For. The errors are not cached, so every request reaches the API. This bypasses the nginx house_api zone, feeds the shared 127.0.0.1 throttle buckets from the first finding without loading any page, and returns the internal API's status codes (200/400/404/429) to the attacker. This applies on both the user and admin hosts; the admin host's middleware matcher excludes _next/.
low.fix: Add the localhost/127.0.0.1:4000 remotePatterns only when NODE_ENV !== 'production' (as is already done for HSTS). In production, rely on same-origin /media paths and set `images.localPatterns` to [{ pathname: '/media/**' }], so the optimizer cannot be pointed at /api/v1/* either.

low.title: No enforced script CSP: the nginx policy is still a Report-Only placeholder, and it already lacks the Kakao postcode script and iframe hosts the frontend now loads
low.evidence: deploy/nginx/snippets/house-csp.conf:2-5: '# PLACEHOLDER policy, sent as Report-Only until the real frontends are built and tested' and `add_header Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only "default-src 'self'; script-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline' https://oapi.map.naver.com ...; frame-src https://www.youtube-nocookie.com https://www.youtube.com; ..."`. Both Next configs send only `frame-ancestors ...; base-uri 'self'; form-action 'self'; object-src 'none'`, with no script-src (apps/web/next.config.mjs:54-57, apps/admin/next.config.mjs:55-58). The frontends are now built and integrated, yet the policy was never enforced. It also omits https://t1.kakaocdn.net from script-src and the postcode iframe origin from frame-src, although apps/web/src/features/w-deal/lib/daum-postcode.ts:10-12 loads that script by default. No report-uri/report-to is set, so the Report-Only header collects nothing.
low.scenario: Any HTML or script injection bug on the user site, broker console or admin console runs without restriction, because nothing enforces script-src, connect-src or frame-src. Combined with the second finding, a single injection on the public site reaches the admin API. If an operator later just renames the header to enforce it as the comment suggests, the 내놓기/구하기 address search breaks, because the Kakao postcode script and iframe are not allowed.
low.fix: Finish the policy and enforce it. Add https://t1.kakaocdn.net to script-src and the Kakao postcode frame origins (postcode.map.kakao.com and the hosts it embeds) to frame-src. Prefer nonces (Next middleware can add a per-request nonce) over 'unsafe-inline' for scripts. Give the admin host a stricter policy (no Naver Maps, YouTube or Kakao hosts; frame-ancestors 'none'). Add a report-to endpoint, run Report-Only briefly against the e2e suite, then switch to Content-Security-Policy.

low.title: ISR breaks view counting: the /complex/[id] page never counts views, while the server-side GET /listings/:id adds fake listing views
low.evidence: Complexes: complex-query.service.ts:89 records a view only on GET /complexes/:id. complex-popularity.service.ts:148 drops bot user agents, and Node fetch's UA 'node' is under 10 characters, so isBotUserAgent returns true. The ISR page reads the complex on the server only (page.tsx:42-48), and ComplexPageView (features/w-complex/page/) never refetches the detail or sends a beacon. fetchComplex is called only from panel/ComplexPanel.tsx:126 and ComplexMapScreen.tsx:87. Listings: listing-query.service.ts:100 calls views.record(viewerKey(principal)) on the server-side GET, and viewerKey gives anonymous Next calls x:hash(127.0.0.1|node). RECORD_VIEW_LUA (listing-views.service.ts:24-35) increments the totals with no bot check, deduplicated for 6 h (constants.ts:6). The client beacon POST /listings/:id/view (features/w-listing/api/client.ts:16) counts real visitors separately.
low.scenario: A visitor arriving from Naver or Google on /complex/<id>, the main SEO landing page, never adds to the 30-day decayed views. So the home ranking of popular complexes (자주 찾는 단지) and the admin's top complexes reflect map-panel usage only. Every listing gets up to 4 fake views a day from the ISR revalidation viewer, which inflates the view counts shown to brokers and owners.
low.fix: Add POST /complexes/:id/view, mirroring the listing beacon, and fire it from ComplexPageView on mount. Make the server-side detail reads side-effect free: skip views.record when the viewer is a bot or loopback, or pass a `?track=0` query parameter or a header from serverGet and stop recording views on the public GET altogether.

low.title: /_next/static assets are proxied to Node and compressed on every request in the Next process
low.evidence: deploy/nginx/snippets/house-web-locations.conf:31-34 sends everything, including /_next/static/*, to `proxy_pass http://house_web`, and the admin locations do the same. apps/web/next.config.mjs does not set `compress: false`, so Next's built-in middleware gzips every JS and CSS response on the fly in the Node event loop. Nothing is precompressed, there is no brotli, and nginx keeps no cache. The web app ships about 1.2-1.4 MB of raw JS per first load (app-build-manifest), and nginx gzip (house-server-common.conf:7-13) never applies because the upstream response already has Content-Encoding.
low.scenario: Cold visitors and every deploy (new chunk hashes) make each house-web instance read the chunks and run gzip level 6 per request. That competes with SSR and ISR rendering on the 2 instances (WEB_INSTANCES default), adds TTFB during traffic spikes, and serves gzip instead of brotli to browsers that support it.
low.fix: Serve static files from nginx: `location /_next/static/ { alias /srv/house/current/apps/web/.next/static/; access_log off; add_header Cache-Control "public, max-age=31536000, immutable"; gzip_static on; }`, optionally precompressing .gz and .br files at build time. Do the same for admin, and set `compress: false` in both next.config files so Node stops compressing what nginx can handle.

low.title: 개인정보처리방침 is modelled as a required consent document, so every policy update blocks all members until they re-consent
low.evidence: TERMS_TYPE_LABEL.PRIVACY = '개인정보처리방침' (packages/shared/src/enums/user.ts:110). Seed: title '개인정보 수집·이용 동의 및 개인정보처리방침', isRequired: true (apps/api/prisma/seed/base.ts PRIVACY entry). /terms/privacy renders this document as the policy (apps/web/src/features/w-content/terms/policies.ts:32-37), and every purpose consent links to it as '개인정보처리방침 전문 보기'. TermsConsentGuard (apps/api/src/modules/auth/terms/terms-consent.guard.ts) returns 403 AUTH_TERMS_REQUIRED on every write until the member re-consents to the current required version.
low.scenario: The operator updates the 처리방침 under 제30조, for example to add a 수탁자 or fix the officer's name. Publishing it makes it a new required version, and every member is blocked from favorites, deal requests and so on until they 'agree' to the policy. Regulators' guidance is that the 처리방침 is something you publish, not something users consent to. Bundling the two makes consent to 수집·이용 (제15조) indistinguishable from reading the policy.
low.fix: Split the two. Keep a required account consent type for 개인정보 수집·이용 (items, purpose, retention, right to refuse), and add a separate non-consent document or policy slug for the 개인정보처리방침. Version and publish the policy without triggering re-consent. Point the footer and auth 'strong' link at it.

low.title: Footer business info has no 호스팅서비스 제공자 (전자상거래법 제10조 / 시행령 제7조)

low.title: Listing JSON-LD gives a monthly-rent-only price, marks reserved listings InStock, and names a region that contradicts D1

Map RESERVED to 'https://schema.org/LimitedAvailability' or omit offers. Take the region from shared DEFAULT_REGION_NAME / sido instead of the '전라남도' literal and BRAND.regionFull.

low.title: 평 is the only area unit on cards, markers and meta descriptions (계량에 관한 법률: 법정단위 ㎡)
